title: RGB Color
story: You're building a design tool and need to represent colors. Every color on screen is made of red, green, and blue values (0-255). You want to compute brightness, check if a color is dark or light, and convert colors to the hex format designers love (#RRGGBB).
why: Color math (average, threshold checks, hex conversion) shows how struct methods can transform raw data into useful derived values.
analogy: A Color is like a paint mixer with three sliders: red, green, and blue. Brightness tells you how much light the mix reflects. is_dark is the question "would white text be readable on this background?" Hex is the universal paint code.
try_it: Add a `Color.invert(self) -> Color` method that returns the complementary color (255 - r, 255 - g, 255 - b). Add a `Color.mix(self, other: Color) -> Color` method that averages each channel. Create your favorite real color.
tips: Brightness is (r+g+b)/3 — integer division drops the decimal, which is fine for threshold checks
Use a string of hex digits and index into it with `n / 16` for the high nibble and `n % 16` for the low
Chain methods: `is_dark` calls `self.brightness()` so the logic stays in one place
common_mistakes: Using lowercase hex digits (a-f) when the exercise expects uppercase (A-F) — check your hex string
Dividing by 3 after casting to Float64 then casting back — Int division works fine for this use case
